paragraphs.text: Less than a quarter of the world’s ocean floor has been mapped in detail. Most existing maps are based on satellite measurements of the sea surface, which reveal large features such as underwater mountains but miss anything smaller than a few kilometres across.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Detailed maps require ships equipped with sonar, which sends sound waves to the seabed and measures how long they take to return. The method is accurate but slow: a single ship would need hundreds of years to map all the oceans.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: An international project now aims to complete a detailed map by 2030. Its organisers ask fishing boats, cargo ships and even private yachts to record depth data as they travel and to share it freely. Uncrewed surface vessels, which can work for months without refuelling, are also being tested.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Better maps have practical uses. They help to predict how tsunamis will travel, show where undersea cables can be laid safely and reveal habitats that may need protection. They may also settle disputes between countries about where their sea borders lie.
paragraphs.label: D
